A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same Qwen2.5/GRPO reinforcement-learning scaling study. Their complete main texts, figures, tables, equations, and appendices are readable and support comparison.

before.justification: v1 reports original RL training experiments, scaling fits, benchmark evaluations, and data-reuse and rollout-size ablations, including appendix results.

after.justification: v2 retains original experimental results and adds larger-model evaluations, extrapolation experiments, and uncertainty summaries.

M1.justification: The proposed predictive scaling model changes substantially: v2 constrains learning efficiency through k(N)=Kmax/(1+N0/N) and introduces an alternative fitted loss-decomposition model in Appendix D. These change the analytical models used to forecast loss. The underlying GRPO algorithm, reward, and model architecture remain unchanged.

E1.justification: Both versions use the same guru-RL-92k mathematics training subset, 500-problem holdout, and mathematics, HumanEval, Zebra Puzzle, and SuperGPQA evaluation coverage. Appendix A.1 retains the same benchmark composition. Larger model sizes and new fitting analyses do not introduce new data or task coverage.

E2.justification: v2 Figure 8 adds explicit comparisons between checkpoints before and after RL across instruction-model sizes; v1's corresponding domain-transfer figures presented training trajectories without separate pre-RL reference curves. The external Qwen3 and GPT-OSS comparator membership is unchanged between v1 Table 6 and v2 Table 4.

E3.justification: The experimental model range expands from 0.5B–14B to 0.5B–72B. v2 adds fitting on models through 32B to predict 72B and forecasting later training from early observations. Appendix D specifies first-30%-of-training fits and two-parameter 72B calibration. Existing benchmark splits, metrics, and GRPO hyperparameters remain unchanged.

E4.justification: v2 adds substantial tests of scaling-law predictability across model sizes and training stages, including the alternative decomposition model (Figures 2, 4, and 13). It removes v1 Figure 13's loss-versus-response-length fit and response-efficiency slopes. The data-reuse and rollout-size ablations are retained; the latter moves to Appendix B.2.

E5.justification: Both versions state that configurations are repeated three times. v2 newly reports average standard deviations and standard errors of the mean for held-out losses in Appendix C.3, Table 5. This adds numerical uncertainty reporting without establishing an increase in repetitions or a new significance-testing procedure.

E6.justification: v2 Table 4 adds 32B Base/Instruct Pass@1 scores of 0.540/0.590 and 72B scores of 0.607/0.617; retained rows match v1 Table 6. New results include larger-model transfer and response-length curves, a reported 32B–72B compute crossover, and extrapolation fits. Earlier per-model slope, intercept, and fit-quality tables are replaced by saturation/decomposition fit results, which are not directly comparable estimates.

T1.justification: v2 introduces explicit saturation functions and Appendix D's mathematical decomposition into irreducible loss, model-limited loss, learnable capacity, and learning progress. It also adds an effective log-log slope definition and a claimed maximal-slope relation and bound in Equation 20. The existing compute–data consistency proof in Appendix C.2 is retained.

C1.justification: The abstract and introduction shift from descriptive larger-model efficiency findings to a predictive scaling law with saturating efficiency gains. The claimed scope expands through 72B, and Observation 1 qualifies larger-model compute optimality by introducing a 32B–72B trade-off. Data-reuse effectiveness remains a core claim.

C2.justification: v1 treats eventual saturation and an optimal model scale as hypotheses for future work. v2 interprets larger-scale results as evidence of efficiency saturation and explains the compute crossover through the trade-off between model size and training steps. Appendix D adds explanations involving pretraining headroom and explicitly acknowledges underdetermined capacity and characteristic-data-scale terms.

D1.justification: v2 identifies Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct as the model used to estimate curriculum difficulty and supplies a code-repository link on the title page. This replaces v1's statement that source code accompanies supplementary material. Existing hyperparameter tables, prompt templates, data identifiers, and FLOPs-accounting instructions are retained.

R1.justification: The cited works and related-work section are substantively unchanged. However, v2 removes v1 Section 3.1's explicit contrast between RL's apparent absence of a compute trade-off and Kaplan/Hoffmann pretraining results, while reporting its own crossover. This changes a limited part of the research positioning.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and central scaling discussion are substantially rewritten around prediction and saturation. Resource-allocation formulations move from the introduction into the corresponding results sections, and the GRPO ablation moves to the appendix. v1's ethics, reproducibility, and LLM-use statements are removed, while the appendices are reorganized around the new decomposition analysis.

P2.justification: Compute/data figures gain extrapolation panels, and new efficiency plots replace earlier slope displays. Domain transfer changes from two 14B training-trajectory panels to an eight-panel comparison before and after RL across model sizes. Appendix tables and figures are added, removed, and relocated, including new decomposition displays and removal of the response-length slope figure. Typography and text width also change throughout.

improvement.justification: The larger-scale experiments expose a compute trade-off that v1 could only anticipate, while explicit pre-RL controls and uncertainty summaries strengthen empirical support. These provide a net benefit, but the gain is limited by removal of per-model fit diagnostics and a flaw in the new theoretical support: Appendix D.3 identifies Equation 20's slope at D0 as maximal, although Equation 19 does not generally place the maximum there.
